title: Chapter 9 — Why The People May Strictly Be Said To Govern In The United States
paragraphs: Up to this point I have examined the institutions of the United States. I have reviewed their legislation, and I have described the current features of political society in that country. But above these institutions and beyond these defining features, a sovereign power exists that can destroy or reshape them at will — I mean the power of the people. It remains to be shown how this power, which regulates the laws, actually operates: what its tendencies and passions are, what the hidden springs are that slow, speed up, or guide its irresistible course, and what effects its unlimited authority produces, along with the destiny probably reserved for it.

In America the people appoints both the legislative and the executive power, and it provides the jurors who punish every offense against the laws. American institutions are democratic not only in principle but in all their consequences. The people elects its representatives directly, and for the most part annually, to ensure their dependence on it. The people is therefore the real governing power. Although the form of government is representative, it is clear that the opinions, prejudices, interests, and even passions of the community face no lasting obstacles and exert a perpetual influence on society. In the United States the majority governs in the name of the people, as happens in every country where the people is supreme. That majority is made up mainly of peaceful citizens who, whether by inclination or by interest, sincerely want the welfare of their country. But they are surrounded by the constant agitation of parties, which try to draw them in and make use of their support.
